title: Multiplatform Build and Release
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of multiplatform build and release using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates multiplatform build and release.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Multiplatform Build and Release** as part of **Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform**. Kotlin Multiplatform organizes shared logic and target-specific implementations through source sets; only APIs available for every configured target belong in common code. Use the subtopics—Building Each Target, Platform-Specific Signing and Packaging, Maintaining Shared Code Safely—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Multiplatform work succeeds when shared code depends only on common APIs and platform-specific code is isolated behind deliberate interfaces.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Kotlin Multiplatform organizes shared logic and target-specific implementations through source sets; only APIs available for every configured target belong in common code.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with building each target. Then compare it with platform-specific signing and packaging. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Building Each Target
items.text: Building Each Target is part of reproducible project configuration. Declare the dependency or plugin where it belongs, preserve a compatible version set, and use the Gradle Wrapper for repeatable builds.

items.title: Platform-Specific Signing and Packaging
items.text: Platform-Specific Signing and Packaging is one part of multiplatform build and release. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: Maintaining Shared Code Safely

content_blocks.code:
data class Greeting(val text: String)

fun greetingFor(name: String): Greeting = Greeting("Hello, $name")

fun main() = println(greetingFor("Kotlin").text)
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run inside a Kotlin Multiplatform project with the target toolchains installed; common and platform-specific source sets have different APIs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Multiplatform Build and Release removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.
